title: Redwood discovery - SigmaTech latency & throughput
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private VPC

SigmaTech needs p95 < 350ms for short chat messages at concurrency 200 and sustainable streaming for 1k tokens sessions; discussed batching, KV cache, quantization tradeoffs, and security (SOC2, KMS, VPC). Next steps: send detailed Dedicated pricing & capacity worksheet, benchmark plan, and request sample prompt distribution.

meeting_header:
Date: 2025-06-15
Time: 16:00 - 16:48 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Jonah Lee (Redwood SE), Lena Carter (SigmaTech CTO), Marco Silva (SigmaTech ML Eng), Priya Narayan (SigmaTech Infra)
transcript:
[00:00] Ava: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Ava from Redwood, AE on this side. Quick intros?
[00:08] Lena: Hi, Lena Carter, CTO at SigmaTech.
[00:11] Marco: Marco Silva, ML eng.
[00:13] Priya: Priya, infra.
[00:15] Ravi: Ravi Patel, SE, I look after performance & benching.
[00:20] Jonah: Jonah Lee, solutions.
[00:22] Ava: Cool. Goal for today: understand your latency p95 targets, concurrency, streaming needs, and whether hosted/dedicated/private fits best. Also any security constraints.
[00:35] Lena: Right. We're evaluating Redwood vs a couple of providers. Our main requirement is p95 under 350ms for short chat messages (~20-80 tokens) at concurrency peaks of around 150-250 concurrent users. For longer streaming sessions up to 1k tokens we need sustained throughput but can tolerate higher p95 like 1s for tail.
[00:58] Marco: To add, our average session generates ~300 tokens, but spike patterns are bursty — we have a few hundred users hitting at once during feature releases. We need predictable cost too, not just best-case latency.
[01:15] Priya: From infra side, we have strict VPC rules and need KMS integration for keys. SOC2 is required — you'll need audit logs and RBAC.
[01:28] Ava: Totally. We can support all of that. Quick clarifying Qs: are you looking for hosted first and then dedicated, or go private from day one?
[01:37] Lena: Prefer hosted to start, but want the option to move to Dedicated or Private within a quarter if latency or data residency issues arise.
[01:45] Ravi: Understood. On the latency p95 target — do you mean end-to-end including network from your clients, or just server-side inference?
[01:52] Lena: Server-side, so from our edge to your inference nodes; we'll add a small hop. But we want your p95 number to include the server processing time.
[02:02] Jonah: Good note. For hosted we publish model-specific p95 numbers on our catalog but they're measured on our infra; we can align measurement methodology during the benchmark.
[02:12] Marco: Can you run numbers for streaming vs non-streaming? We need both.
[02:16] Ravi: Yep. Streaming changes the latencies — initial token first-byte times matter and then tokens/sec sustained throughput. Can you share typical message lengths and percentiles?
[02:24] Marco: Sure — 50% under 80 tokens, 30% 80-300 tokens, 15% 300-800, 5% >800.
[02:34] Ava: Great, that's helpful. For short messages our KV cache and prefix caching help reduce repeat context. For longer sessions batching and quantization profiles affect throughput. We usually characterize workload by tokens/sec and tokens per request distribution.
[02:50] Lena: What's realistic tokens/sec on Dedicated? We heard numbers like 1k-2k tokens/sec per GPU for some models.
[02:58] Ravi: It depends on model family, sequence length, and quantization. For a 7B-ish model with int8 quant we typically see ~1k-3k tokens/sec per GPU for streaming scenarios under continuous decoding. For 13B or 70B family numbers drop. But we can run a mini-benchmark with your payloads to show exact figures.
[03:20] Marco: For p95 under 350ms, do you need lower compute or special placement?
[03:25] Jonah: Achieving sub-350ms p95 for short responses typically needs single-token latencies in the ~50-150ms range server-side and very low queueing. That implies small queue sizes, reserved capacity or Dedicated with autoscale buffers, and model variants optimized for latency (quant+pruned configs).
[03:42] Priya: Network jitter matters for us — can Redwood dedicate capacity in a region close to our users? We are mainly in NA-east.
[03:49] Ava: Yes, Dedicated and Private can be pinned to regions. Hosted also has regional edge routing but Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools closer to your endpoints.
[03:58] Lena: Cost — how does dedicated compare to hosted? If we reserve capacity, what's the deal on utilization?
[04:05] Ravi: Dedicated is a reservation model: monthly commit for a pool. Unit cost per token goes down with reserved capacity but you pay for idle as part of the commit. We provide autoscale and burst to reduce wasted capacity. Hosted is pay-as-you-go with slightly higher per-token cost but no commit. We'll send a capacity/pricing worksheet.
[04:22] Marco: For benching, what do you need from us?
[04:25] Ravi: Sample prompt sets, typical concurrency distribution, representative session durations, and whether you need streaming partials or only final outputs. Also, sample payloads (10-50) and a small script to replay concurrency patterns. If you can't share real data we accept synthetic distributions.
[04:42] Marco: We'll share synthetic but realistic traces.
[04:45] Priya: Security again: do you support customer-managed KMS and audit logs for Private?
[04:51] Ava: Yes, Private supports customer KMS/HSM integration and we surface audit logs; Dedicated has options for encryption at rest with customer-managed keys and per-token logging controls. We'll attach the security whitepaper.
[05:05] Lena: Regarding SLA — do you have p95 SLA?
[05:08] Jonah: We have latency-backed SLAs for Dedicated and Enterprise tiers; hosted has generalized SLAs. Specific p95 SLAs can be discussed as part of the enterprise contract.
[05:18] Marco: Can you share previous benchmark results?
[05:20] Ravi: We'll share a couple of anonymized benchmark spreadsheets; those are usually model-level with sequence length distributions and tokens/sec. Expect variations.
[05:30] Lena: Great. On the tech: what's the caching behavior? If a lot of requests share prefixes, how much does that help p95 at scale?
[05:39] Ravi: Prefix and KV cache reduce compute per token when there's repeated context. In chat apps that reuse system prompts or similar histories, we can shave 20-60% off compute for repeated tokens, which helps p95 and cost. But cache hit rates depend on your prompt entropy.
[05:55] Marco: For concurrency 200, do you recommend Dedicated?
[05:58] Jonah: For consistent p95 SLAs at that concurrency and needing sub-350ms, Dedicated is the safer bet. Hosted can do spikes but you may see higher tail latency under noisy neighbor or capacity constraints. We also provide capacity tiers to mitigate.
[06:11] Priya: Is there a middle ground — reserved bursts?
[06:14] Ava: Yes, burst pools and autoscale policies let you keep base reserved and burst out to shared capacity for infrequent spikes.
[06:22] Marco: When you say tokens/sec per GPU, is that measured with continuous decoding only or does it include streaming overhead?
[06:28] Ravi: Typically continuous decoding with streaming enabled; we can separate initial token latency and sustained tokens/sec. Streaming adds small overhead for chunking and network chunk latency.
[06:37] Lena: About model variants — do you recommend quantized variants for latency targets?
[06:41] Ravi: Often yes. Int8 or mixed int8/16 quant profiles reduce latency and memory footprint. There's a small quality delta; we can run quality checks vs your eval prompts.
[06:53] Marco: That leads to quality monitoring — can you set up evals and regression alerts?
[06:57] Jonah: Redwood Optimize integrates with eval sets and can trigger regression alerts per model/version. We'll demo in the deep dive.
[07:05] Ava: Quick check — do you have any regulatory data residency reqs?
[07:09] Lena: No not yet, NA-only fine.
[07:12] Priya: Maybe later, but not blocking.
[07:15] Marco: For benchmarks, can you emulate our burst pattern: 10 minutes high QPS, 30 minutes baseline?
[07:21] Ravi: Yes, we'll provide a load harness and run it in one of our dedicated pools or in hosted with a warmup period.
[07:30] Lena: How do you measure p95 across streaming vs non-streaming? We want consistent definitions.
[07:36] Jonah: We'll measure server-side processing time per request for non-streaming; for streaming we'll report time-to-first-byte and time-per-token percentiles and aggregate into a p95 equivalent for initial response. We'll share measurement methodology doc.
[07:48] Marco: Any gotchas we should know for long context (8k+)?
[07:52] Ravi: KV cache and chunked attention optimizations help; but memory use increases. For very long contexts we often recommend model variants with optimized attention kernels or a retrieval-augmented approach to avoid feeding entire long histories every time.
[08:06] Priya: For Private deployments, what's the uplift on ops? Do you manage the control plane?
[08:12] Ava: Private gives a customer-managed data plane; we offer an optional managed control plane or self-managed. There's an on-prem package for air-gapped. ETA and pricing vary by region.
[08:22] Lena: Ok. Can you summarize the benchmark plan now?
[08:25] Ravi: Sure. Steps: 1) SigmaTech shares sample prompts and concurrency profile; 2) Redwood runs three phases — cold/warm single-user latency for p50/p95, steady-state tokens/sec throughput under sustained decoding, and burst concurrency test; 3) compare hosted vs dedicated configs; 4) provide a spreadsheet with tokens/sec, p50/p95, and cost per 1M tokens estimates.
[08:47] Marco: Sounds good. What tools will you use to replay traffic?
[08:50] Ravi: We use locust-based harness and a custom client to simulate streaming chunking. We'll share the runbook.
[08:57] Priya: For security review, we need SOC2 docs and encryption at rest details.
[09:01] Ava: We'll attach SOC2 and security whitepaper. We'll note KMS/HSM options for Dedicated/Private.
[09:08] Lena: Any third party vendor approvals needed?
[09:11] Ava: Not usually, but we'll sign an NDA if needed.
[09:14] Marco: For the benchmark, can you run both int8 quant and fp16 so we can see quality vs perf?
[09:19] Ravi: Absolutely, we'll include quant profiles.
[09:22] Jonah: One more note — we'll instrument tracing hooks so you can correlate request IDs with latency spans.
[09:29] Lena: Excellent.
[09:31] Ava: Quick pause — anyone have pressing constraints we haven't covered?
[09:35] Priya: Network egress limits for our VPC, but that's typical.
[09:39] Marco: No, good.
[09:41] Ava: OK, I'll recap and next steps at the end. Let's fast-forward through some deeper Qs: model sizing, queueing, and batching.
[09:50] Ravi: On batching: batching improves throughput but increases tail latency due to queueing. We tune batch windows and max batch size to hit p95 targets. For sub-350ms p95 we cap batch window low and rely on more reserved capacity.
[10:05] Marco: What's a typical max batch size?
[10:08] Ravi: Depends, but for low-latency use cases we keep small batches (1-4 requests) and rely on parallelism across GPUs. For throughput-focused workloads we increase batch sizes.
[10:19] Lena: How do you handle KV cache eviction under high concurrency?
[10:22] Jonah: We do LRU-ish policies and also shard caches by session to avoid eviction storms. We'll show cache hit stats in the bench report.
[10:33] Marco: For cost modeling, can we get per-token cost with reserved vs hosted assumptions?
[10:37] Ava: Yes, the pricing worksheet will have sample scenarios and cost per 1M tokens estimates for each model & deployment type.
[10:44] Priya: On RBAC — can we map to our SSO groups?
[10:47] Jonah: Yes, we support SAML/SSO and can map roles to groups.
[10:51] Lena: Great. Any questions from Redwood?
[10:54] Ravi: Just one: what would be the success criteria after the bench? Is p95 < 350ms the single gate?
[11:00] Lena: It's primary gate for short messages. Secondary is tokens/sec >= X for our 1k token sessions — we want sustained >500 tokens/sec for long sessions across pooled capacity. Also cost per 1M tokens under a threshold.
[11:13] Marco: We'll define exact numbers in the doc we share.
[11:17] Ava: Perfect. Let's plan the deep dive week of 6/23. We'll run a hosted benchmark first and then a dedicated run if needed.
[11:27] Priya: Sounds good.
[11:29] Ava: Recap: Ava send pricing & capacity worksheet, Ravi send benchmark plan + runbook, SigmaTech share sample prompts and concurrency traces, schedule SE deep dive.
[11:40] Lena: Thanks all.
[11:42] Ava: Thanks, we'll follow up in email with attachments and calendar invite.
[11:46] [Meeting ends]

Note: Transcript contains occasional ASR errors and speaker tag mis-assignments typical of auto-transcripts. Shared artifacts mentioned: Dedicated-pricing-workbook.xlsx (link sent), benchmark-runbook.md (link to internal runbook), anonymized-benchmarks.csv.
